source.title: Advisory on the Use of Chinese Money Laundering Networks by Mexico-Based Transnational Criminal Organizations (FIN-2025-A003)

summary: GOLDEN LABEL, hand-drafted against the PDF. FinCEN advisory on how Chinese money laundering networks (CMLNs), professional launderers operating as unregistered MSBs and brokers in the Chinese underground banking system, launder drug proceeds for the Sinaloa, CJNG and Gulf cartels and other Mexico-based TCOs. The core mechanism is a mirror transaction: a U.S.-based CMLN takes the cartel's USD cash, a Mexico-based counterpart pays pesos into the cartel's Mexican accounts, and the USD is resold to Chinese citizens who pay RMB inside China to evade PRC currency controls, so no funds cross a border. Supporting techniques are recruited money mules (students, diaspora) with counterfeit passports, smurfing across branches, cashier's checks, P2P and wire layering, real estate purchase, CVC as an alternative settlement rail, and a TBML leg in which mules and daigou straw buyers purchase electronics and luxury goods that shell, front or complicit businesses resell or export to Mexico, China, Hong Kong and the UAE, sometimes to cartel-owned companies in place of a mirror transfer. One case study (Operation Fortune Runner, Martinez-Reyes) and nineteen red flags; pages 11-15 are BSA reporting obligations.

typologies.label: Mirror-transaction currency swap through Chinese underground banking (BMPE-style, no cross-border movement)

citations.quote: in which an equivalent amount of pesos is transferred to the Cartels’ Mexico-based accounts, minus a nominal fee.  Through this informal value transfer, CMLNs “purchase” the value of the Cartels’ illicit USD proceeds in pesos.
This RMB transfer internal to China avoids the PRC’s currency control laws and effectively “purchases” the control of the USD from the CMLN.

typologies.label: Export of purchased luxury goods as value exchange in place of a mirror transfer

citations.quote: In some cases, U.S.-based CMLNs may export these goods to Cartel-owned companies in Mexico as an alternative to a mirror transfer.  These exports serve as a form of value exchange between CMLN operators that avoids cross-border money movements
CMLNs may use money mules and other recruits to purchase U.S. electronics and other luxury goods ( e.g., cell phones, automobiles, clothing, designer handbags, etc.) at various

typologies.label: Surrogate shopping (daigou) straw buyers acquiring and shipping U.S. goods to China

citations.quote: CMLNs typically provide the daigou buyer with cash or send a P2P transfer to their account and instruct them to purchase certain goods.  The daigou buyers are also instructed to ship the goods to a location in China or to a daigou operator
CMLNs may use money mules to deposit the illicit USD into accounts they are directed to open at U.S. depository institutions, or at accounts held by U.S.-based Chinese nationals or businesses.

They may also deposit the illicit funds into existing money mule accounts ( i.e., personal or shell company accounts) and then use wire, automated clearing house (ACH), or peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers to send the money to separate accounts held by U.S.-based Chinese nationals and businesses.
CMLN money mules may also engage in “smurfing” operations 35 across multiple depository institution branches to deposit illicit funds into money mule accounts
“structuring,” that is, depositing small amounts at a time into bank accounts opened for this purpose to avoid banks from reporting large cash deposits to the U.S. government.
across multiple depository institution branches to deposit illicit funds into money mule accounts, or into accounts held by U.S.-based Chinese nationals and businesses.

A customer, especially a Chinese national, regularly deposits large volumes of cash or cashier’s checks, or receives multiple wire, ACH, or P2P transfers for no business or apparent lawful purpose.  The customer then subsequently uses the funds to purchase a cashier’s check or disperses the funds to other individuals using P2P and wire transfers
The money mules may also purchase cashier’s checks from depository institutions with U.S.-based Chinese nationals and businesses listed as the payee directly.
A customer, especially a Chinese national, has large amounts of cash funding cashier’s checks, which are then deposited at another financial institution.

A customer’s account, especially a Chinese national, receives numerous transfers or deposits, and has a significant number of withdrawals or transfers, none of which appear to be related to routine payroll, living expenses, or customer’s stated expected activity.
Such businesses may have income that is not commensurate with that of other businesses of a similar size.
A business that sells electronics or other luxury goods has income that is not commensurate with the size and scale of the business.
Once the goods are purchased, CMLNs often use shell or front companies, or complicit businesses, to resell or export these goods in a variety of ways.

Hong Kong registered trading companies with shell-like characteristics send funds to Chinese nationals residing in the United States, real estate escrow or title insurance companies, and other international destinations with no apparent business or economic purpose.
These purchases may be made using the drug proceeds or with credit cards that are subsequently paid off by the CMLN or by the complicit business owner.
A business that sells electronics or other luxury goods makes payments for multiple credit cards associated with various individuals, who are seemingly unrelated to the business.

Alternatively, CMLNs may purchase cashier’s checks listing the payee as a shell company the CMLNs beneficially own or listing the payee as a U.S.-based company or individual in the real estate industry.

A customer that is a U.S.-based escrow company receives funds from an unaffiliated, foreign-based shell company or entity in a disparate line of business that are used to purchase real estate in the United States.

CMLNs also coordinate and network with CMLNs or PMLs in other countries through IVTS and TBML to launder illicit proceeds, which obviates the need to physically transport cash or execute cross-border wire transfers.
These exports serve as a form of value exchange between CMLN operators that avoids cross-border money movements and serves as a revenue source for the CMLNs.

typologies.label: Convertible virtual currency as an alternative settlement rail for mirror transactions

citations.quote: CMLNs may also use convertible virtual currency (CVC) as an alternative means to conduct mirror transactions with the Cartels.
Additionally, the remitters also moved illicit drug proceeds through cryptocurrency transactions.

typologies.label: Counterfeit passports and fake identity documents supplied to mules for account opening

citations.quote: such as the provision of fake identification documents to individuals opening bank accounts on their behalf.
CMLNs may also provide money mules with counterfeit Chinese passports to facilitate account opening and engage in other illicit financial behavior.

actors.name: Chinese money laundering networks
actors.role: Professional money launderers of Chinese nationals, U.S.- and foreign-based, operating as unregistered MSBs and brokers in the Chinese underground banking system

citations.quote: According to Treasury’s 2024 National Money Laundering Risk Assessment, CMLNs are one of the most significant money laundering threat actors facing the U.S. financial system.
CMLNs typically comprise both current and former U.S.- and foreign-based Chinese passport holders ( i.e., Chinese nationals).

actors.name: Mexico-based transnational criminal organizations
actors.role: Cartel clients who sell their illicit USD drug proceeds to CMLNs for laundering; designated FTOs and SDGTs under E.O. 14157

citations.quote: the Cartels sell off their illicitly obtained USD to CMLNs who, in turn, sell the USD to Chinese citizens seeking to evade the PRC’s currency control laws.

actors.name: Jalisco New Generation Cartel
actors.role: Named cartel using CMLNs to launder drug proceeds

citations.quote: by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), the Sinaloa Cartel, the Gulf Cartel, and other Mexico-based transnational criminal organizations (TCOs)

actors.name: Sinaloa Cartel
actors.role: Named cartel; its Los Angeles-based associates are the subject of the Operation Fortune Runner case study

citations.quote: charging Los Angeles-based associates of Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel with conspiring with money-laundering groups linked to Chinese underground banking to launder drug trafficking proceeds.

actors.name: Gulf Cartel
actors.role: Named cartel using CMLNs to launder drug proceeds

citations.quote: by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), the Sinaloa Cartel, the Gulf Cartel, and other Mexico-based transnational criminal organizations (TCOs)

actors.name: CMLN money mules
actors.role: Recruited Chinese diaspora members and students on U.S. visas who open accounts, deposit cash, structure and buy cashier's checks; witting or unwitting

citations.quote: CMLNs often recruit members of Chinese or other diaspora populations to participate in their money laundering operations to act as money mules, 11 money brokers, and cash couriers.
CMLNs may target individuals on student visas in particular, since such individuals are often restricted from obtaining certain types of lawful employment in the United States.

actors.name: Daigou buyers
actors.role: Current or former Chinese nationals in the U.S. who buy goods on CMLN instruction and ship them to China or to a daigou operator; witting or unwitting

citations.quote: Daigou buyers may be witting or unwitting individuals and may be current, or former, Chinese nationals residing in the United States.

actors.name: Complicit U.S. businesses and financial institution insiders
actors.role: Retailers that sell goods for drug cash or pay off mule credit cards, and bank employees recruited or placed by CMLNs

citations.quote: CMLNs may sell goods in the United States through various online marketplaces, at front companies, or at businesses complicit in their schemes.
CMLNs may also recruit financial institution employees to act as complicit insiders or infiltrate and place CMLN members within a financial institution to assist in CMLN operations.

actors.name: Edgar Joel Martinez-Reyes
actors.role: Lead defendant in Operation Fortune Runner; Los Angeles-based Sinaloa Cartel associate who struck the deal with Chinese underground banking remitters

citations.quote: Lead defendant Edgar Joel Martinez-Reyes and others allegedly used a variety of methods to hide the money’s source, including trade-based money laundering, “structuring” assets to avoid federal financial reporting requirements, and the purchase of cryptocurrency.

actors.role: California-based money transmitting group linked to Chinese underground banking that processed over $50 million of Sinaloa Cartel drug proceeds

extraction_notes: Golden label. Printed folio equals the PDF index on every page. Pages 11-15 are BSA reporting, due diligence and information-sharing boilerplate with no typology content. The mirror transaction is the advisory's central mechanism and has no governed home: it is an IVTS swap, not trade, so it is emergent under family other (as ADV-2026-0008's BMPE entry) rather than tbml; the advisory's own SAR box (36(l) TBML/Black Market Peso Exchange) is the reason the name says BMPE-style. The goods-export leg is a separate emergent tbml entry because the advisory says exports substitute for a mirror transfer; daigou kept as its own emergent label for consistency with ADV-2026-0001. CMI010 not used: the CVC content is laundering, not sanctions evasion, so emergent under crypto as in ADV-2026-0001/0003. BA001 rests on 'smurfing' (p6) and 'structuring' (p8); the p6 quote keeps the inline footnote marker '35' verbatim. BA002 is the weaker of the mule-account pair: deposits across many branches into one account then dispersed by P2P and wire fit the funnel shape, but the advisory never uses the term, so medium. BA008 rests on cashier's checks re-deposited at a second institution and wire/ACH/P2P onward moves; medium. TBML009 covers shell and front companies reselling or exporting goods and the HK shell-like trading companies red flag; PAT007 not labelled separately (same evidence, TBML framing). TBML008 is the most contestable governed entry: CMLN or complicit-business payoff of mule credit cards is a third-party payer settling a purchase, kept at medium because it appears in the typology section and again as a red flag. Real estate purchase through mules and shell companies (p6, case study p8, three red flags) is deliberately not a typology: the library has no home and it is integration of proceeds rather than a distinct technique; reviewer may promote it. Colombian peso brokers and shadow banking networks (p1) and healthcare fraud and illicit gaming (p4) are mentioned once and not labelled. Chinese citizens buying USD to evade PRC currency controls are the demand side and customers, not threat actors; not labelled. Enforcement bodies (FinCEN, Treasury, DOJ, DEA, HSI) are not actors. CMLN jurisdiction is CN by nationality, as AZ was used in ADV-2026-0017, although the networks operate in the U.S. Jurisdictions are US (where the cash is laundered), MX (cartel side of the swap), CN (RMB leg and PRC currency controls), HK and AE (export counterparties and shell trading companies, p7 and p10); Colombia is an actor origin mentioned once and excluded.  Indicators left empty per slice 1.  RE-CHECKED 2026-09-11 under the restated indicator rule: pp9-10 are FinCEN's red-flag groups, so one bullet now supports a typology. ADDED, all medium: BA005 (p9 — numerous deposits, significant withdrawals, none matching stated expected activity: through-volume vs normal profile, not BA003's controller relationship); BA010 (p7 'businesses of a similar size', p10 'not commensurate with the size and scale of the business' — peer segment, not threshold); PAT007 (declined before as TBML009's evidence; these citations are not the trade leg — CMLN-owned shell as cashier's-check payee p6, foreign shell funding a real-estate escrow p10); PAT009 (p4 CMLNs coordinating with PMLs abroad through TBML, p7 exports as 'value exchange between CMLN operators'; the emergent export entry stays, PAT009 not carrying the mirror-transfer substitution). DECLINED on mechanism: BA007 (placement is via mule personal accounts, not a business's own cash), BA009 (the p10 marketplace flag is a front company selling real goods, not card-rail processing for others), BA004 (fn31 replenishes peso supply between operators; nothing returns to origin), PAT010 (control of accounts, not of an organisation), SAN008 (doctrine excludes jurisdiction as an aggravating detail, all p9 offers), SAN004 (framed as laundering, not sanctions evasion). Nothing removed or downgraded. Governed 6 to 10.
